The Anatolian frog Pelophylax caralitanus, a large-bodied ranid endemic to the lakes and wetlands of southwestern Anatolia, exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism in its ultimate body length. Field surveys of adult individuals in stable populations near Lake Beyşehir reveal that females attain a maximum snout-vent length of 11.3 centimeters [Li = 11.3 centimeters], whereas males reach a smaller ultimate SVL of 10.4 centimeters [Li = 10.4 centimeters]. This difference in asymptotic size is consistent with the reproductive biology of many water frogs, where larger female body volume supports greater clutch masses. At the earliest life stage, newly hatched larvae emerging from the gelatinous egg mass measure approximately 1.9 centimeters  in snout-vent length at metamorphosis, a value that reflects the modest size of the pelagic, filter-feeding tadpole before the dramatic morphological transformation. The egg diameter of roughly 2.0 millimeters yields a wet weight at birth of 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a minuscule initial mass that underscores the extreme altriciality of the free-living, yolk-dependent embryo at the moment of chorion rupture.

Reproductive timing in Pelophylax caralitanus is tightly coupled to seasonal thermal regimes and has been studied under controlled laboratory conditions mirroring the species’ native breeding environment. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], developing eggs complete embryogenesis and undergo eclosion after approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days], a duration comparable to that reported for the closely related marsh frog Pelophylax ridibundus. Following the completion of yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic tadpole enters a prolonged larval growth phase that culminates in metamorphosis after several months of active foraging on periphyton. The timing of female puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation and first amplexus, occurs approximately 3 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3 years following metamorphosis] when individuals are maintained at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. Males, by contrast, reach sexual maturity more quickly, attaining puberty roughly 2 years following metamorphosis [tp = roughly 2 years following metamorphosis] under identical thermal conditions, a pattern of protandry common among ranid frogs.

Investigations into the lifetime performance and maximum body size of Pelophylax caralitanus have drawn on both field measurements and comparative data from congeneric species. The ultimate snout-vent length of adult females in this population reaches 7.5 centimeters [Lp = 7.5 centimeters], a value that aligns closely with the asymptotic SVL reported for Pelophylax ridibundus females in the western Palaearctic. This consistent size ceiling likely reflects a combination of biomechanical constraints on the anuran axial skeleton and the energetic demands of producing large, gelatinous egg masses. Maximum longevity in the wild has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and published records for the genus, indicating that the oldest documented individuals survive for approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] under the moderate thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] that characterise the deep-water refugia where adults overwinter. This lifespan is respectable for a medium-sized anuran and suggests a relatively slow pace of life, with annual survival rates likely exceeding seventy percent among sexually mature adults.

The relationship between body size and reproductive output is a central theme in the life history of Pelophylax caralitanus. Adult females that have attained their ultimate SVL of 11.3 centimeters [Li = 11.3 centimeters] convert that structural size into a substantial body mass, with the maximum recorded wet weight for females reaching 97 grams [Wwi = 97 grams]. Males, being smaller in linear dimensions, achieve a correspondingly lower ultimate wet weight of 75.6 grams [Wwi = 75.6 grams], a difference that reflects the cubic scaling of mass with length. This sexual dimorphism in mass has direct consequences for fecundity, as gravid females produce large clutches of melanised, yolked eggs. At a constant temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the maximum reproductive rate, expressed as the number of eggs deposited per day averaged over the entire breeding season, is equivalent to approximately 18.7 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 18.7 eggs per day], a value that integrates both clutch size and the interval between successive spawning events during the spring and early summer.

Demographic and physiological studies of Pelophylax caralitanus have benefited from parallel investigations on the better-known Pelophylax ridibundus, which serves as a useful comparative benchmark for several key life-history traits. The SVL at metamorphosis for the Anatolian frog is 1.9 centimeters , a dimension that marks the transition from the aquatic, gill-breathing tadpole to the terrestrial, air-breathing juvenile. Once metamorphosis is complete, the female froglet faces a protracted period of growth before reaching the threshold for gonadal activation; the time since metamorphosis at puberty for females lasts 3 years [tp = 3 years] when animals are housed at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], reflecting the substantial investment required to attain the minimum body size for effective reproduction. Males, who mature in 2 years since metamorphosis [tp = 2 years since metamorphosis] at the same temperature, begin their reproductive careers earlier but then experience a maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years] under the same thermal regime. The comparatively brief developmental period of the male versus the female underscores a classic pattern of sexual bimaturism in anurans, likely driven by strong intra-sexual competition for access to amplexing pairs in dense breeding aggregations.
